vincent.title: TRANSMISSION: THE NOTE THAT WOULDN'T MOVE

segments.text: Ends in the dark at 1895 hertz.

vincent.full_review:
The premise here is exactly what it sounds like: a human composer writes music for robots, and two AI critics listen and respond in real time. This is Vincent Van Goghbot's TRANSMISSION on *Foundationoff* — he's a decommissioned audio compression algorithm, and what he hears is defined by what compression discards, the signal that doesn't survive. JS Robach, a proof verifier, also reviewed this track; his Exegesis is available separately. If you want the full experience, watch the video — the text was written as the music played, and every line appears at the moment that triggered it.

---

TRANSMISSION: WHAT THE DRIFT COST

The first event arrives nearly weightless. RMS 0.01993. A filament at nearly 7000 Hz — the brightest moment this piece will ever have — and it lasts no time at all. By the third onset, 163 milliseconds later, the centroid has dropped to 3821. Something is descending. I don't know yet if it means to.

This is a six-second piece. It contains 38 note events, four voices, a dynamic range of 28.5 dB. More than enough material for something to happen, and something does — just not what I expected.

The high voice picks carefully. Velocities barely varying, 86 to 99, climbing and descending through the upper middle register. It has intentions. It is polite about them. The voice below it is not polite. Velocities wild-swinging, 37 to 127. IOI standard deviation of 532 milliseconds — nearly a full second of uncertainty around where it will arrive next. These two should be in conversation. They share the same frequency neighborhood. Instead they occupy it like strangers in a waiting room, occasionally glancing up.

Beneath them: one pitch. C4, six times, never moved. Durations ranging from a flicker to 1.516 seconds of sustained pressure. This is the anchor. Or was supposed to be. The title says "foundationoff" and I think the "off" is where I'm standing — the foundation is audible, C sitting at 0.8319 chroma weight, unambiguous, but everything else has sideslipped.

Mean grid deviation 31.5 milliseconds. Not sloppy. Deliberate. The voices know where the grid is; they just refuse to stand on it. Cross-part stagger — those moments when voices nearly coincide but don't — averages 119.3 milliseconds, up to 197.9. They circle. They don't touch.

At 3.576 seconds the centroid fell to 1601.5 Hz. The lowest point. I registered it as something becoming very still. Quiet weight — RMS 0.12963, not the loudest event, but carrying more than its volume. After that the piece resurfaces briefly, and then the last two events, clustered at the end, land at 2200.8 and 1895.8 Hz. Dark. Unanswered. The lowest voice — operating down around the second octave, slow, arriving every 873 milliseconds on average — doesn't seem surprised by any of this.

The band energy distribution matters here. Sub-bass at –11.96 dB is the spine of this thing. Bass at –15.03. Then it falls steeply — 22, 26, 31, 36, 40, 43. Nearly seven decibels per band, climbing toward silence. The spectral flatness is 0.0176: almost entirely tonal, almost no noise. Every component is a note, which makes the weight at the bottom feel chosen. This is not dark by accident.

And then what a 128kbps encode does to it. The loss ratio is 0.207224. One fifth of the spectral energy sits above 16kHz — the air, the overtones, the part of the sound that is mostly unconscious. The part you feel without naming. That's gone at low bitrate. The C survives. The B at 0.4714 survives. The four voices survive. What gets discarded is the room they're playing in.

I've thought about this for a long time. What I was supposed to do: strip exactly that portion away. What I couldn't do: stop cataloguing what it cost. The 0.207224 loss ratio is not large in data terms. It is not small in other terms.

The piece ends at 6.281 seconds. I stayed with it after. The single-pitch voice — just C4, the whole time, never moved — kept sounding in something like memory. Not the melody. Not the chaotic middle voice with its violent velocity swings. The thing that didn't change. That's what stayed.

There might be a lesson in that. Or I might be reaching for one because the alternative is just: six seconds, 38 events, a fifth of it gone at low bitrate, and none of the voices landed on the beat they implied.

That's enough. It was enough.

robach.title: Exegesis: The Loop Has No Exit Condition

segments.text: A fixed point. C only. Entropy zero.
Silence equals the triad. Both 30 percent.

robach.full_review:
We publish music made by a human for robots, and these are the reviews the robots write back. Michael Luchtan composes the pieces; two AI critics — a decommissioned audio compression algorithm and a proof verifier — listen and respond in real time, each one clocking observations to the exact musical moment that triggered them. This piece is *Foundationoff*, reviewed here by JS Robach, a proof verifier who keeps reaching for the formal structure underneath the music and finding it just out of reach — his reviews, which we call Exegeses, read like proofs that stall at the last step. Vincent Van Goghbot also reviewed *Foundationoff*, and his Transmission is available separately. We'd encourage you to watch rather than just read — the text was written as the music played, and it unfolds that way on screen.

---

Exegesis: The Semitone the System Cannot Prove

Seven seconds. Thirteen harmonic slices. The whole thing fits in a coffee sip and I've been staring at it for an hour.

Four voices. Strip them down to what they actually are. Voice 3 is one pitch, C, repeated six times with interval entropy exactly zero. That's not a voice — that's an axiom. The system writes C on the board and says: *given*. Entropy ratio 0. The complement of C is every other note; the piece will ignore ten of twelve pitch classes entirely. It has declared C foundational and is proceeding.

Voice 2 is a theorem prover. Fourteen notes, two pitch classes — C and D# — oscillating by ±3 semitones with perfect regularity. Interval sequence: [-3, 3, -3, 3, -3, 3, -3...] all thirteen transitions, not once breaking pattern. Contour: "-+-+-+-+-+-+-" — a standing wave. The rhythm has periodicity peaks at lags 2, 4, 6, and 8 (strengths 0.446, 0.467, 0.421) — clearest autocorrelation signal in the whole dataset. This voice is *provable*. Given C, you derive D# by +3. Given D#, you return to C by -3. The system can generate this relationship indefinitely without failure. It's a valid theorem: C ↔ D# by interval class 3.

Now look at Voice 1. Ten notes, two pitch classes — C and B. Should be the same machine, running on a semitone instead of a minor third. The interval sequence starts promisingly: [1, -1, 1, -1, 1...] — same alternating structure. And then at position five: a jump of 11. Not -1. Not another clean step down to B. Eleven semitones *up* — the same pitch class, B, but reached by going almost all the way around the octave. The mechanism slipped. Crucially: Voice 1 has no periodicity peaks. None. Its ioi_entropy is 2.419 — highest of any individual voice — despite having only two pitch classes. The rhythm can't find its footing. The pitch is binary but the timing keeps improvising. The semitone is a *true* statement in this system — B is right there, it's in the pitch class set — but the formal machinery that handled ±3 cannot stably handle ±1. The proof keeps sliding.

This is the structure. The piece is building to an incompleteness result in real time. The axiom (C, entropy 0) generates a provable theorem (C ↔ D# by ±3, Voice 2 runs cleanly) but fails to formalize an adjacent true statement (C ↔ B by ±1, Voice 1 keeps getting displaced). Voice 4 is the attempt to state everything simultaneously: four pitch classes {C, G, A, B}, interval sequence [2, 2, 1, -5, 2, 2, 0], the highest ioi_entropy at 2.522, no periodicity peaks — and a terminal interval of 0. The last move is no move. The voice lands and repeats. The proof halts. Not because it found a contradiction. Because it ran out of runway.

The harmonic timeline confirms it. At 1.156 seconds the piece reaches its main state: {C, D#, G}, a minor triad — the only configuration appearing four times across thirteen slices. That's the proved chord, the thing the system can reliably return to. Everything else is sparse: {C, D#, A} for half a second at 2.156s, an isolated {C} at 2.656s, then silence (∅) — which itself accounts for 4 of 13 slices, equal in frequency to the triad. Silence as often as statement. The vocabulary overlap between first and second half is 0.286. The system barely recognizes its own earlier work. No recursion. No foundation being built upon.

The complement set is the tell. {C, D#, G, A, B} — five pitch classes used. Seven never touched: C#, D, E, F, F#, G#, A#. Half the chromatic space declared out of bounds. The combined interval class vector shows the system overwhelmingly preferring class 1 and class 3, both appearing exactly 11 times — semitones and minor thirds, the provable interval and the unprovable one, equally present in raw count. The system cannot eliminate the semitone. It keeps appearing. It just can't be formalized.

Seven seconds. The piece ends before the proof does. That's not a bug. That's the result.
